newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian student march seeks diplomats' support.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian student march seeks diplomats' support.

text.p: About 2,000 Bulgarian students marched through Sofia on Monday delivering petitions to Western embassies urging support for the opposition's call for a general election.

The Promyana trade union launched a series of one-hour warning strikes and the opposition planned nationwide rallies later in the day as daily protests inspired by severe economic crisis entered their second week.
The protesters, marshalled by student security officers, sang, danced and chanted slogans. Drama students turned out in theatre costumes.

"We do not want to join the immigrants to your countries, we want a new life here and now," said a declaration delivered to the Italian, Austrian and U.S. embassies, referring to the many young Bulgarians who leave to seek a better life abroad.
The students appealed to embassies not to support any new government of the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP), which is half way through its parliamentary term.

The Promyana trade union said miners in the Rhodope mountains were expected to join the dockers on Tuesday. A general strike would be held next week if the Socialists did not yield to the opposition's demands.

"We are preparing a nationwide strike but we would not want to go ahead with it because the economy is in a bad state as it is and such a strike will finish it off," Dimitar Dimanov, deputy president of Promyana, told Reuters.

After demonstrators besieged parliament for 10 hours on Friday and Saturday, Zhelev declined to ask the Socialists to form a new government to replace that of Prime Minister Zhan Videnov, who resigned on December 21.

Legally, Videnov's government remains in office until a replacement is formed, but quick formation of a new government is vital to secure a new funding agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and avert default on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt.

Bulgarian Brady bonds fell on the secondary debt market on Monday and traders said they were concerned that the unrest would delay establishment of a tough fixed exchange rate regime proposed by the IMF to stabilise the economy.
The pro-government speaker of parliament, Blagovest Sendov, said the Socialist party, which includes leading ex-communists, should agree to the opposition's demands.
"I am convinced that there is no time to waste and this problem should be solved immediately," Sendov said.
Socialist leader Georgi Parvanov said he was happy to discuss elections but the formation of a new Socialist government was a priority.

The main opposition trade union Podkrepa said it would join the strike action on Wednesday, and other trade union organisations also expressed support. Under Bulgarian law, full strikes require a week's notice.

The French foreign ministry appealed for dialogue. "We are following the situation in Bulgaria with all the more concern because this country is an associate of the European Union and furthermore a member of the Francophone movement," said foreign ministry spokesmn Jacques Rummelhardt.
Voters delivered a powerful no-confidence vote two months ago by electing opposition lawyer Petar Stoyanov as president with 60 percent of the vote. He will be sworn in on January 19.

Annual inflation for 1996 was 310.8 percent, and the Socialists' critics blame the party's powerful business allies for unchecked capital flight which has helped push the lev down to 642 to the dollar from 70 a year ago.
